newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND - Global bond markets face subdued 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Global bond markets face subdued 1997.

text.p: Bond investors had a lucrative year in 1996 but some analysts say the smile on debt investors' faces may be wiped away in early 1997.
"We're bearish, particularly for the first half of next year," said Graham McDevitt, senior analyst at Paribas Capital Markets.

Tame inflation, tighter budgets and looser monetary policy, coupled with slow growth and a frantic drive to meet European Union economic convergence criteria have all helped to push European debt markets to new all-time highs.
And while the U.S. Treasury market had an uncomfortable start to the year, receding growth rates in the second half of 1996 helped the market regain much of its early losses.

But there is a risk in the United States that inflationary pressures from earnings -- which is not easy to stem swiftly -- will begin to filter through early in 1997 and push the Federal Reserve towards an interest rate rise, analysts said.

Speculation on the future direction of U.S. rates has see-sawed throughout 1996, with tight labour market data and strong growth figures in the first half leading to numerous predictions that policy would have to be tightened.
That talk has died down as growth slowed and the feared signs of inflationary pressure failed to materlialise but some analysts believe bond investors should beware.

"Even though growth figures have slowed a bit in the last few months, it is quite clear that the inflation risk is still very high -- not so much from producer or consumer prices but from earnings," said McDevitt. "That is where the focus of the markets will be."
In Europe, a pick-up in German and pan-European growth was likely to show, prompting markets to discount interest rate rises in the latter half of 1997, McDevitt said.
"We're looking for the (German) repo rate to start moving up in the third quarter."
Economists at Salomon Brothers agreed the outlook for European bonds was shaky for the year ahead.
Sustained economic recovery, the bottoming of the inflation cycle and concerns about the implications of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) were all factors pointing to higher yields.
By the end of next year the yield on the 10-year benchmark Bund should be flirting with 6.5 percent compared with 5.9 percent currently as debt prices come under pressure, Salomon said.

High-yield markets such as Italy, Spain and Sweden, which this year have earned investors big returns on convergence plays -- which speculate on the likelihood that the economies and financial instruments of candidates for EMU will converge successfully -- are also seen facing a less exciting time.
"The risk/reward tradeoff in Europe's high-yielding bond markets is substantially less attractive than a year ago," Salomon said in its 1997 outlook.
But it added that convergence was not yet entirely dead and pointed to further outperformance in markets such as Spain Portugal and Finland.
Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International, was far less bearish on global bonds.

"Global inflation is tame and is likely to remain so throughout 1997. Budgets are being reined back in the U.S., Japan and Europe. Global growth will stay around trend or if anything a bit weaker," he said.
"Those who are looking for a major sell-off in 1997 are premature."
With EMU talk continuing to pervade European markets, U.S Treasuries would appear to be the best of the heavyweight markets for bond bulls in 1997, analysts said.

While McDevitt said the risk of wage pressure would add to the need for monetary tightening in the United States, both Chester and Joanne Collins, senior economist at Nomura International, said interest rates were more likely to be trimmed in 1997, supporting T-bond buyers.
Collins said Nomura was forecasting a reduction by 25 basis points (a quarter of a percentage point) in the key Federal Funds rate by the middle of next year.
"We're still optimistic for T-bonds," she said.
